articles.title: What to do while you wait
articles.summary: Waits for assessments and services can be long. Here are practical things families can start now: support at school, parent groups, free workshops, and funding you can apply for early.
articles.body_markdown:
Waiting for an assessment, or for services after one, can take a long time in many parts of Canada. The Canadian Paediatric Society has noted that a one-size-fits-all team approach to autism assessment "contributes to long wait times".

The wait doesn't have to be empty time. Here are things families can start now. Most of our examples are from Ontario, and we say so each time. Other provinces have their own versions, so ask what exists where you live.

## Ask about support at school now

In Ontario, a school can write an Individual Education Plan (IEP) for a student who hasn't been formally identified as "exceptional", when the student needs special education support to attend school, meet curriculum expectations or show what they've learned. Ontario's special education categories also include conditions "whether diagnosed or not".

If you think your child needs an IEP, Ontario suggests talking with your child's teacher or the school's special education teacher about how to start one. A few examples of what you see at home can help that conversation.

## Find other parents

Talking with parents who've been through the same wait can make it feel less lonely, and they may know which local services are worth a call.

- CADDAC, a national ADHD charity, runs free virtual parent support groups. The facilitators are parents and caregivers of children with ADHD themselves.
- In Ontario, once your child is registered in the Ontario Autism Program (OAP), foundational family services are free. They include family and peer mentoring, and caregiver workshops with follow-up coaching.

## Learn for free

- Autism Ontario's Signature Series webinars are free, live interviews for autistic adults, parents and professionals. Past episodes can be watched on demand.
- CADDAC keeps a library of free past webinars about ADHD.

Some people find one short webinar a week is plenty. There's no need to learn everything before the appointment.

## Apply early for funding

Some applications take a while, and some don't need a final diagnosis.

- In Ontario, Special Services at Home (SSAH) asks for documentation of your child's need for extra support from a regulated health professional. For infants and young children, where a diagnosis can be hard to pin down, the professional can describe the "probability or presence of delay" instead.
- Across Canada, the disability tax credit (DTC) form can be sent to the Canada Revenue Agency at any time of year, and a medical practitioner fills in part of it. An approved DTC is what the Child Disability Benefit needs, so it's a useful first step.

Our article "Help paying for services: what to check first" goes through these in more detail.

## Ask about lists

In Ontario, autism can be diagnosed by doctors (including family doctors and pediatricians), psychologists and psychological associates, and nurse practitioners. You can also contact one of Ontario's five diagnostic hubs.

Some families ask whether they can be on more than one waitlist, for example a hub and a private clinic, and whether a clinic keeps a cancellation list. Not every clinic allows this, but it's always fine to ask.

If your child already has a diagnosis: in Ontario, children are invited into the OAP's core clinical services in the order they registered, so it helps to register as soon as you have the written diagnosis.

## Keep a simple folder

During an autism assessment in Ontario, the professional reviews documents and earlier reports, including information from a school or childcare provider. Some parents keep report cards, notes from teachers and a short list of what they notice at home in one folder, so it's ready when the appointment comes.

## Where to start

1. Ask your child's teacher what support is possible at school now.
2. Join one parent group, online or nearby.
3. Ask each clinic about cancellation lists and whether you can be on more than one list.
4. Start one funding application, like the disability tax credit or, in Ontario, SSAH.

articles.title: Help paying for services: what to check first
articles.summary: The disability tax credit opens the door to the Child Disability Benefit, the RDSP and the Canada Disability Benefit. Here is what each one is, plus Ontario examples, and why it helps to apply early.
articles.body_markdown:
Therapy, equipment and respite add up. If you're not sure where to begin, here's what we'd check first. The first four are federal and work the same across Canada. For provincial programs we use Ontario as the example; other provinces have their own, so ask your province what exists.

## 1. The disability tax credit (DTC)

The DTC is a non-refundable tax credit that lowers the income tax a person with a disability, or their supporting family member, may have to pay. You may apply if there is a severe and prolonged impairment. The application has two parts, and a medical practitioner certifies one of them.

The DTC matters beyond tax time: the Child Disability Benefit, the RDSP and the Canada Disability Benefit all depend on it. That makes it a good first application.

## 2. The Child Disability Benefit

This is a tax-free monthly payment for families caring for a child under 18 with a severe and prolonged impairment. Your child needs to be eligible for the DTC, and you need to be eligible for the Canada child benefit.

If you already get the Canada child benefit, you don't apply separately: it comes automatically once the DTC is approved. The first time, the CRA also works out payments for the current and two previous benefit years.

From July 2026 to June 2027, it's up to $3,480 a year ($290 a month) for each eligible child. It starts to go down when adjusted family net income is above $82,847.

## 3. The Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP)

An RDSP is a long-term savings plan for people approved for the DTC. You open one at a financial organization and apply for the grants and bonds at the same time.

- **The grant** matches what you put in. It's up to $3,500 a year, with a lifetime limit of $70,000.
- **The bond** is for people with low and modest incomes, and you don't have to put any money in to get it. It's up to $1,000 a year, with a lifetime limit of $20,000.

If the DTC was approved for earlier years, you may get extra grant and bond money for up to the past 10 years. This is called a carry-forward.

## 4. For adults: the Canada Disability Benefit

The Canada Disability Benefit is for people with disabilities aged 18 to 64 who have been approved for the DTC. Payments began in July 2025, and everyone who meets the requirements can now apply online. From July 2026 to June 2027, the most it pays is $204.20 a month.

Teens can apply up to 6 months before their 18th birthday. Filing taxes every year matters here too: payments need a filed tax return.

## 5. Provincial programs: Ontario examples

- **Assistance for Children with Severe Disabilities (ACSD)** pays between $25 and $678 a month toward disability-related costs.
- **Special Services at Home (SSAH)** funds things like respite and support for your child to join activities at home and in the community.
- **The Ontario Autism Program (OAP)** is for children and youth with a written autism diagnosis. Foundational family services, like caregiver workshops, are free for every registered family.

## Income and waits, plainly

Some programs look at family income and some don't. The Child Disability Benefit, the RDSP's grants and bonds, the Canada Disability Benefit and ACSD all depend on income in some way. ACSD, for example, is for households with an income of $77,640 or less. Eligibility for the DTC depends on the impairment, and eligibility for the OAP depends on age, living in Ontario and a written diagnosis.

Some programs also have waits. Children enter the OAP's core clinical services in the order they registered, and SSAH funding depends on available resources. So it helps to apply early, and to apply even if you're not sure you'll qualify. If an application is turned down, ask what comes next: ACSD, for example, lets you ask for an internal review within 30 days.

## Where to start

1. Ask your child's doctor or another medical practitioner about the DTC form (T2201).
2. Once the DTC is approved, check that the Child Disability Benefit has started, and ask a bank or other financial organization about opening an RDSP.
3. In Ontario, look at ACSD and SSAH, and register with AccessOAP if your child has an autism diagnosis.

articles.title: Starting college or university: your accessibility office
articles.summary: Your accessibility office sets up accommodations like test arrangements and note-taking. Here is what it does, what documentation schools ask for, why to register before classes start, and a federal grant to know about.
articles.body_markdown:
Starting college or university means a lot of new systems at once. One worth finding early is the accessibility office. It arranges academic accommodations for students with disabilities and ongoing medical conditions, and its name changes from school to school: Accessibility Services at the University of Toronto, the Centre for Accessibility at UBC, and Student Accessibility & Achievement at McGill. If you're starting college, look for the same kind of office on your college's website.

## What the office does

The office works with you to explore which accommodations fit, and connects you with other support. At U of T, you and your accessibility advisor develop a Letter of Accommodation, which you use to start the conversation with course staff.

Your information stays private. At UBC, you don't have to share information about your disability with your instructors or any other UBC office, and your transcript won't show that you're registered with the Centre.

## Examples of accommodations

U of T lists examples like these:

- writing quizzes, tests and exams through its Accommodated Testing Services
- note-taking support, one of the most common accommodations
- textbooks and readings in other formats, like Word or e-text
- extensions on assignments, asked for before the original due date
- a reduced course load

## What they usually ask for

Each school sets its own rules, so read your school's page. Three examples:

- **University of Toronto:** registration has three steps: get documentation, fill in an online intake form, then go to an intake appointment. For most students, the documentation is U of T's Certificate of Disability, completed by a health care practitioner who is licensed to make a diagnosis. A diagnosis is requested but not required. If you're still getting documentation, the office can talk through what you're experiencing and suggest referrals for an assessment.
- **UBC:** medical documentation from a professional who is qualified to diagnose your condition. If yours is out of date or hard to get, you can explain that when you book. In exceptional circumstances, the Centre can discuss limited accommodations without documentation.
- **McGill:** book an appointment with an advisor and upload your medical documentation, which needs a clear diagnosis or clinical description. McGill has a referral form your professional can fill in. If you had accommodations before, send proof of those too.

At U of T and McGill, accommodations are based on how your condition affects your studies, not on a diagnosis alone. The offices don't diagnose, but they can help you find where to ask.

## Start before classes begin

Registering takes time, so it helps to start early:

- U of T lets you register as soon as you've accepted your offer of admission, and encourages registering before classes begin.
- McGill encourages new students to book an appointment before their first semester, so supports are in place when classes start.
- UBC describes registration as a multi-step process that can take some time.

Once you're registered, check whether you need to confirm your accommodations each term. At McGill, students review and confirm them at the start of every semester.

## Money for school

The Canada Student Grant for Students with Permanent Disabilities is $2,800 a year until the end of the 2026 to 2027 school year, for students with financial need. You apply at the same time as your provincial or territorial student aid, with a document that shows your disability. There's also a separate federal grant for services and equipment.

## Where to start

1. Find your school's accessibility office page and note what documentation it asks for.
2. Ask your doctor or other professional for that documentation early, since appointments can take a while.
3. Register as soon as you accept your offer, before classes begin.
4. Apply for the disability grant when you apply for student aid.

articles.title: The autism timeskip: what changed in 15 years
articles.summary: From four diagnoses to one, more adults assessed, autistic people's word choices, and new supports in Canada: a short, sourced look at what's different since around 2011.
articles.body_markdown:
If you were diagnosed, or first wondered about autism, around 2011, a lot has shifted since. Here's a short tour of what's different now: the diagnosis itself, adult assessments, language, and support in Canada. We've kept to what official sources and autism organizations say.

## The diagnosis: from four names to one

**Then:** the DSM, the manual many clinicians in Canada use, had four separate diagnoses on the spectrum, including Asperger's and PDD-NOS.

**Now:** in 2013, the American Psychiatric Association published the fifth edition, DSM-5. It brought all four under one umbrella, autism spectrum (ASD), and grouped communication and social interaction into a single area. Its severity levels are based on how much support a person needs.

If you were diagnosed with Asperger's or another older name, Autism Ontario says you should still meet the criteria for ASD in DSM-5. You can keep using whichever word fits you.

## Adult diagnosis: more common now

Autism Ontario says assessments in adulthood are becoming more common, because the criteria have broadened and awareness and understanding have grown. It also notes that a diagnosis can be a validating experience that helps adults understand themselves. Whether to seek one is a personal choice.

In Ontario, adults are generally diagnosed by a psychiatrist or a psychologist. Psychiatrists are covered by OHIP. Psychologists may be covered when they work in a public setting such as a hospital; private psychologists charge fees, which work benefits or other private insurance may cover. Autism Ontario lists adult assessment providers by region.

National numbers are still mostly about young people. When it announced its autism framework in 2024, the Government of Canada gave an estimate of 1 in 50 children and youth aged 1 to 17 diagnosed with autism, and said it was exploring ways to measure and report on autism in adults.

## Language: autistic people's preferences count

Autism Ontario's language statement says many in the autistic community prefer identity-first language ("autistic person") over person-first language. It recommends identity-first language and uses both, and it notes that language keeps evolving. The federal government's 2024 autism framework announcement talks about supporting "Autistic people of all ages".

People choose their own words. In Autinerary, you can pick yours in Settings, under Words we use.

## Support in Canada

**Federal, now:**

- The Framework for Autism in Canada and Canada's Autism Strategy were released on September 26, 2024. They were developed with Autistic people, families, caregivers, provinces, territories and Indigenous organizations.
- In March 2025, the government announced funding for a new National Autism Network, led by the Sinneave Family Foundation in partnership with Autism Alliance of Canada.
- The Canada Disability Benefit began paying in July 2025. It's for people with disabilities aged 18 to 64 who are approved for the disability tax credit. From July 2026 to June 2027, it's up to $204.20 a month.

**Ontario, then and now:**

- In 2019, Ontario held public consultations on autism services and formed an advisory panel, which included adults on the autism spectrum, to advise on a needs-based program.
- Today, families register through AccessOAP, the program's independent intake organization, and behaviour plans are no longer offered.
- The Ontario Autism Program still ends at 18. For adults, Autism Ontario points to options like the Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP), Passport funding for adults with a developmental disability, the disability tax credit and the Canada Disability Benefit.

## The balanced view

Plenty has moved: one diagnosis instead of four, more adults assessed, more say for autistic people in the words used, and new federal plans and benefits. Some things move more slowly. Adult assessments in Ontario can still mean a private fee, and the provincial program for children stops at 18. Knowing both helps you plan.

## Where to start

1. Curious about an adult assessment? In Ontario, you can ask your doctor or nurse practitioner for a referral to a psychologist in a public health care setting, or to a psychiatrist.
2. If you have the disability tax credit, look at the Canada Disability Benefit.
3. Pick the words that fit you in Settings, under Words we use.

articles.title: Asking for accommodations at work
articles.summary: Employers in Canada have a legal duty to accommodate. Here's what you can ask for, how to start the conversation, and why you usually don't have to share a diagnosis.
articles.body_markdown:
You can ask for changes at work that help you do your job well. In Canada, human rights law backs this up, and it's called the duty to accommodate.

## Which law covers you

- **Federally regulated employers**, like banks, air and rail transportation, Crown corporations such as Canada Post, and the federal public service, follow the Canadian Human Rights Act. They have a legal duty to accommodate, up to the point of undue hardship.
- **In Ontario**, the Human Rights Code gives employers a legal duty to accommodate the needs of people with disabilities, also up to undue hardship.

If your employer isn't federally regulated and you're outside Ontario, your province's or territory's human rights commission is the place to check.

## What you can ask for

The commissions' own examples include:

- a flexible work schedule
- more frequent check-ins with your supervisor
- changes to your workstation, or assistive technology for your computer
- other ways of communicating with you
- changes to some duties
- working from another location, or telework

Some people also ask for a quieter spot to work, headphones, or instructions in writing. Start with what would make the biggest difference.

## Starting the conversation

It's usually up to you to tell your employer that you need an accommodation. Often it can be a simple conversation, without a formal request. Ontario's commission suggests sharing your needs in writing where you can, which also gives you a record.

You don't need to explain everything. The federal guide says you only need to tell your employer what gets in the way at work; suggesting what would work can help too. It also says employers should have clear procedures for requesting accommodation, so it's fine to ask HR or your manager how it works.

## You usually don't have to share a diagnosis

Under the Canadian Human Rights Act, you don't have to disclose a specific diagnosis when you ask for a disability-related accommodation, and employers are very rarely entitled to it. In Ontario, an employer generally doesn't have the right to know your diagnosis either, unless it clearly relates to the accommodation or your needs are complex or unclear.

Your employer may still ask about your needs or limitations, sometimes with information from a health care provider. That's about what you need, not your diagnosis.

## Where to start

1. Write down two or three changes that would help most.
2. Find out whether your employer is federally regulated, or covered by your province.
3. Ask HR or your manager how to request accommodation, and follow up by email.
